1100.title: Raga Ramkali
1100.hook: a calm morning raga, home of Guru Nanak's talks with the yogis, that opens by setting learning aside for the one Name
1100.howItsDone: Shabads from the Ramkali section of the Guru Granth Sahib are sung in kirtan in Raga Ramkali, which Sikh musical tradition associates with a calm morning mood.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a hymn in Gond: a frightened driver, a judge who didn't see, and an elephant that did. Your line: the elephant bowed. A new week starts.

Some read Sanskrit. Some read the old Puranas. Some sit with a string of beads, counting the Name, fixed in meditation. That's how today's raga begins, on ang eight seventy-six of the Guru Granth Sahib: a quick tour of serious religious people doing serious religious things. A listener might expect the next line to pick a winner. It doesn't. Guru Nanak steps out of the lineup altogether, and what he says next is very quiet. Today: Raga Ramkali.
screen: `SANSKRIT, PURANAS, BEADS.` → `A LINEUP OF THE DEVOUT.` → `NANAK STEPS OUT OF IT.`

segments.voice: Ramkali follows Gond in the Granth's order, and Sikh tradition hears it as a calm morning raga. First, the opening hymn's turn, in paraphrase: I know nothing, now or ever; I recognize only your one Name. Then the refrain: I don't know, Lord, what my state is. And: I'm foolish and without understanding; I've come to your shelter; be kind, and keep my honor. No reader is mocked, no bead-counter is scorned. Guru Nanak simply doesn't compete. Where others show what they know, he admits what he doesn't, and rests in the Name. That's the calm. Second, the yogis. Ramkali is where the Granth holds Guru Nanak's talks with the yogis, the wandering ascetics with their earrings, horns and begging bags; tomorrow brings the Sidh Gosht, his long conversation with them. In another Ramkali hymn, Guru Nanak takes up their own gear, in paraphrase: awareness of the Word is my horn, and the world hears it sound; honor is my begging bag, and the Name is the alms I receive. Tradition says the yogis honored a master called Gorakh. The hymn's refrain answers: the true Gorakh is the One who lifted up the earth and made it without delay. Third, together. In Ramkali the outward signs of religion, scholarship, beads, earrings, horns, are each turned inward and pointed at the Name. Nothing is thrown away; everything goes deeper. Calm and deep.
screen: `RAMKALI FOLLOWS GOND.` · `I RECOGNIZE ONLY YOUR ONE NAME.` · `THE WORD IS MY HORN.` · `EVERY OUTWARD SIGN TURNED INWARD.` · then, large: `CALM AND DEEP.`

segments.voice: Let the breath slow until it's barely noticeable, then for two minutes set down whatever you know, what you've read, what you believe, what you'd argue for, not thrown away, just placed beside you. Sit with one word, or with nothing, the way a still lake sits under the morning, letting Waheguru be that word if you pray.
Raga Ramkali. The calm morning raga after Gond, home of Guru Nanak's talks with the yogis, which opens with I recognize only your one Name. Today's word.
Your line: calm and deep. The Word is the horn the world hears. Rest well.

1101.title: A hymn in Ramkali
1101.hook: Ramkali holds the Anand, the Sadd, the Oankar and the Sidh Gosht: bliss, a farewell, an alphabet and a debate
1101.howItsDone: Sikhs sing part of the Anand Sahib, from Raga Ramkali, at the close of congregational gatherings, and the Sidh Gosht, the Oankar and the Sadd are read and sung from the same section of the Guru Granth Sahib.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Raga Ramkali, where Guru Nanak steps out of the lineup and rests in the one Name. Your line: calm and deep.

One heading, Raga Ramkali, and under it, a song of bliss. A few pages on, a deathbed and a farewell. A few more, an alphabet poem that talks back to a teacher. Then a long debate with yogis, seated in their circle. If a raga is a room, this one has guests from a celebration, a funeral, a schoolroom and a yogis' circle, all on the same carpet. Today: a walk through that room, and one hymn to listen to.
screen: `ONE HEADING, MANY GUESTS.` → `A CELEBRATION, A FAREWELL, A SCHOOL.` → `AND THE YOGIS' CIRCLE.`

segments.voice: First, the Anand, Guru Amar Das's song of bliss, on ang nine seventeen. It opens, in paraphrase: bliss has come, my mother, for I have found the True Guru. Sikhs sing part of it at the close of gatherings, so the end of a service sounds like that first line. Second, the Sadd, a few pages on, a poem by Sundar. It tells how Guru Amar Das, near his death, called his family together and told them not to weep for him. When I'm gone, he says in the poem, let the Lord's praises be heard instead. And he places Ram Das as the next Guru. A farewell that asks for songs, not tears. Third, the Oankar, Guru Nanak's alphabet poem, beginning from Oankar, the One who brought forth creation. Its refrain speaks to a pandit, a teacher: listen, pandit, why write down the world's tangles? Write the Lord's Name instead. Fourth, the Sidh Gosht, Guru Nanak's conversation with the Siddhas, the yogis. They open with blunt questions, in paraphrase: who are you, what's your name, what's your path, what are you after? And the long answer comes back, again and again, to the Word and the Name. So this path calls Ramkali the richest raga. Not because its music is better than the others, but because one heading holds a celebration, a farewell, a lesson and a debate, and every one ends up at the same place.
screen: `THE ANAND: BLISS HAS COME, MOTHER.` · `THE SADD: SONGS, NOT TEARS.` · `THE OANKAR: WRITE THE NAME.` · `THE SIDH GOSHT: WHO ARE YOU?` · then, large: `THE RICHEST RAGA.`

segments.voice: If you can, play the opening of the Anand, often found as anand bhaiaa meree maae, and let it run; if not, take the yogis' first question slowly for yourself: who are you? Don't answer with your job or your name; let the question sit, then let the Anand's first line answer it in its own way, bliss has come, with one Waheguru if you pray.
A hymn in Ramkali. One raga holding the Anand's bliss, the Sadd's farewell, the Oankar's alphabet and the Sidh Gosht's debate, all pointed at the Name. Today's word.
Your line: the richest raga. Bliss, a farewell, a lesson and a debate, all ending at the Name. See you tomorrow.

1102.title: Nat Narain
1102.howItsDone: In kirtan, Sikh musicians sing the shabads of the Nat Narain section in that raga; the raga named at the head of a hymn in the Guru Granth Sahib gives the musical color it is sung in.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a hymn in Ramkali, and your line was the richest raga. Today the color changes.

At a wedding, the dhol player picks up the pace, and before anyone decides to, feet are moving under the tables. Some music won't let a body sit still. The Guru Granth Sahib has a raga this path hears in that key. It's a short section, tucked in after the long, calm rooms of Ramkali, and its name is Nat Narain. So what does a lively raga do with devotion?
screen: `FEET MOVING UNDER THE TABLES.` → `AFTER RAMKALI, A SMALL ROOM.` → `NAT NARAIN.`

segments.voice: Narain is a name for God, and here it's part of a raga's name. The hymns gathered under it belong to Guru Ram Das, the fourth Guru, and Guru Arjan, the fifth. The section opens with Guru Ram Das talking to his own mind. In plain English, not word for word: my mind, repeat the Lord's Name day and night, and countless wrongs are set aside. He isn't lecturing a crowd. He's turning to himself, the way you'd turn to a friend who keeps drifting off mid-conversation. That habit runs all through Gurbani: the mind gets spoken to directly, coaxed, encouraged, sometimes scolded. In a lively raga, the coaxing has a bounce in its step. The Granth gives devotion many moods, a raga for each, and one of them is lively. The same Name sung slow and heavy in one section comes back quick and bright in another. The raga sets the color; the Name stays the same. And the liveliness isn't decoration. In kirtan, the music carries the words; it doesn't cover them. A bright tune that buries the hymn has missed the point. A bright tune that gets a tired mind back on its feet has found it. That's today's line: lively.
screen: `NARAIN: A NAME FOR GOD.` · `MY MIND, REPEAT THE NAME.` · `DEVOTION HAS MANY MOODS.` · `THE TUNE CARRIES THE WORDS.` · then, large: `LIVELY.`

segments.voice: Sit up tall and, for a few breaths, breathe a little brisker than usual, the way you'd breathe walking up a short hill, or skip that part if it doesn't suit you. Then let the breath settle back to its own pace and stay with it. If you pray, say Waheguru on each out-breath, the way Guru Ram Das turns to his mind, again and again; if you don't, count your out-breaths to ten and begin again.
Nat Narain. A short, lively raga of the Guru Granth Sahib, where Guru Ram Das turns to his own mind and says: repeat the Name, day and night. Today's word.
Your line: lively. Sometimes a drifting mind just needs a friendly voice saying: come on, once more. Until tomorrow.

1103.title: Listening in Nat Narain
1103.hook: a lively raga for a slow listen
1103.howItsDone: Sikhs listen to kirtan in the gurdwara, at home and through recordings, and many follow along with the words of the Guru Granth Sahib, often with a translation on a screen or in a book, so the music and the meaning arrive together.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nat Narain, and your line was lively: a Guru turning to his own mind and saying, once more.

Speed hides things. A fast song comes on in the car, and the first time through, you catch the beat and not much else. Somewhere around the third play, a line you'd been half-singing comes clear, and it isn't what you thought. Speed is wonderful, and it still hides things. So today, something slightly odd: one hymn from a lively raga, listened to slowly.
screen: `THE BEAT FIRST.` → `THEN THE WORDS COME CLEAR.` → `A LIVELY RAGA, LISTENED TO SLOWLY.`

segments.voice: This Nat Narain hymn is by Guru Arjan, the fifth Guru, and in plain English, not word for word, it opens: I lay no complaint against anyone; whatever you have done is sweet to my mind. Heard quickly, over a bright tune, that can slip past as a pleasant line. Heard slowly, it asks a great deal. No complaint against anyone. Not the coworker, not the relative, not the delayed train. The hymn isn't claiming nothing hard ever happens. It describes a person who has stopped keeping a file of grievances, because what comes is received as the Creator's doing and tasted as sweet. Guru Arjan sings the same thought in Raga Asa: what you do seems sweet to me. Sikhs speak of this as living within hukam, the divine order, and taking it as sweet. That's a big idea to hear at speed. So the practice this path gives for Nat Narain is to listen twice: once letting the music lift you along, then again following the words, line by line. The two listens don't compete. Kirtan holds the liveliness and the depth at once; a listener sometimes needs two passes to catch up. Slowing down isn't correcting the raga. It's letting the words land after the music has opened the door. That's today's line: slow the lively.

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and bring to mind one small complaint from this week, the kind that replays on its own, and just let it be there. Then set Guru Arjan's line beside it, no complaint against anyone, without arguing and without forcing an answer, and breathe with the two side by side. If you pray, say Waheguru slowly on the out-breath; if you don't, simply keep breathing.
Listening in Nat Narain. Hearing a lively raga twice: once for the music, once for words like Guru Arjan's, I lay no complaint against anyone. Today's word.
Your line: slow the lively. Some lines only open up on the second pass. I'll be here tomorrow.

1104.title: Mali Gaura
1104.howItsDone: Each raga section of the Guru Granth Sahib is sung in its own raga in kirtan; shorter sections like Mali Gaura are drawn on just as the longer ones are, and a single shabad is a complete offering in a gurdwara program.

segments.voice: Yesterday, listening in Nat Narain, and your line was slow the lively: once for the music, once for the words.

A postcard holds a few lines and a stamp. Nobody calls it a failed letter. Sometimes it's the thing that stays on the fridge for years, because it said one thing and said it well. Past Nat Narain in the Guru Granth Sahib, you come to a section with a postcard's size and its own full heading: Mali Gaura. It's short. It's complete. And it has a guest at the end.
screen: `A POSTCARD, NOT A FAILED LETTER.` → `A SHORT SECTION, ITS OWN HEADING.` → `MALI GAURA.`

segments.voice: First, Mali Gaura gets the same treatment as the long ragas: its own name at the top and an invocation of the One, Ik Onkar, Satgur Prasad, the One Creator, known by the Guru's grace. A short raga isn't an appendix. In the Granth, a few pages can be a whole room. Inside, the voices are Guru Ram Das and Guru Arjan, and then, closing the section, Bhagat Namdev, a devotee whose hymns the Gurus gathered into the Granth beside their own. His verse is for tomorrow. Today, the opening. Guru Ram Das begins, in plain English, not word for word, with a picture of seekers: adepts, searchers and silent sages, all turning their minds toward the Lord with longing. It's a wide view for a small room. People known for hard practices are shown with the same longing anyone can have, and the hymn's answer is that the Guru shows them the unseen Lord. That's the sweetness of a short raga. No time to wander. It names the longing, points to the answer, and stops. Length isn't the measure here; a short shabad sung with attention is a complete offering. Mali Gaura says what it came to say, then hands the last word to a guest. That's today's line: short and sweet.

segments.voice: Choose one short word to stay with: if you pray, Waheguru; if you don't, simply the word here. Say it once, silently, and let it be complete, without stacking more words behind it. When the mind starts writing a longer letter, set the pen down and come back to the postcard: one word, one breath, each time enough on its own.
Mali Gaura. A short raga of the Guru Granth Sahib, with its own heading and invocation, where Gurus sing first and Bhagat Namdev closes. Today's word.
Your line: short and sweet. A few words, said with attention, can be a whole offering. Until tomorrow.

1105.title: Listening in Mali Gaura
1105.hook: listen to one hymn and its Bhagat verse
1105.howItsDone: Hymns of the Bhagats, like Namdev's, are sung in kirtan in their raga just as the Gurus' hymns are, and many listeners follow the Gurmukhi text with a translation on a screen or in a book while it is sung.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mali Gaura, and your line was short and sweet. The guest at the end of it gets today.

Blessed is the wool. That's a line from the Guru Granth Sahib. Not blessed is the temple, not blessed is the king. Blessed is the wool, and the blanket made from it. It comes near the end of Mali Gaura, in the first hymn of its guest, Bhagat Namdev. So today, reading along with him slowly: why would a saint bless a sheep's coat?
screen: `BLESSED IS THE WOOL.` → `THE GUEST AT THE END.` → `READ ALONG WITH NAMDEV.`

segments.voice: Namdev's hymn starts with music. In plain English, not word for word: blessed, blessed is that flute the Lord plays; the sweet, sweet sound rings out, unstruck. That line is marked Rahao, pause, and in Sikh reading the Rahao line is the center the rest of the hymn turns around. Then Namdev starts blessing things. Blessed is the wool of the sheep. Blessed is the blanket Krishna wraps around himself. Blessed is mother Devaki, in whose home the Lord was born. Blessed is the forest of Brindaban. Namdev is singing from inside the stories of his own world, the cowherd Krishna with his flute, and Sikhs read these names as names for the one God the whole Granth praises. Watch the direction. Namdev doesn't stay with the grand things. He goes to the wool, the blanket, a mother's house, a forest. The holy, in this hymn, makes everything near it holy too: the ordinary cloth, the ordinary home. It's short enough to hear end to end in one sitting, and with the words in front of you, you can watch it walk outward from the flute to the wool. The word for sweet here is madhur, and Namdev doubles it: madhur madhur. So yesterday's line turns around. Mali Gaura was short and sweet. Namdev's verse is sweet and short.

segments.voice: Let your eyes rest on whatever is closest, a sleeve, a cup, the chair, and notice it with care: where it came from, whose hands touched it before yours. Namdev blessed wool and a blanket; let this ordinary thing be quietly important for a minute. If you pray, say Waheguru as you look at it; if you don't, just keep your attention on it, gently.
Listening in Mali Gaura. Reading along with Bhagat Namdev's verse: the flute's sweet, sweet sound, and blessings on the wool and the blanket. Today's word.
Your line: sweet and short. In Namdev's hymn, even a blanket sits close to the holy. More tomorrow.

1106.title: Raga Maru
1106.hook: the raga of courage, traditionally sung before battle
1106.howItsDone: Shabads from the Maru section are sung in Raga Maru in kirtan. Sikhs recite the Mul Mantar, with its words nirbhau and nirvair, at the start of daily prayer, and it stands at the opening of the Guru Granth Sahib.

segments.voice: Yesterday, listening in Mali Gaura, and your line was sweet and short: Namdev blessing the wool.

Calm and deep. Lively. Short and sweet, with a blanket blessed. All week the ragas kept changing color. Now the mood turns. The next section of the Guru Granth Sahib is Raga Maru, and tradition says it was sung before battle, when people needed their nerve. It's a hard mood to sing about: being afraid, and going anyway.

Maru is a long section, and it holds hymns that look hard things in the face: death, loss, the shortness of a life. Tradition remembers it as a raga for the eve of battle. Its hymn is for tomorrow. Today, the color itself: courage. To hear what courage means here, go back to the Granth's first page. The Mul Mantar, the root statement, names the One with a short list. Among its words are nirbhau, without fear, which you met on day 544, and nirvair, without hate. They sit side by side. The courage the Granth honors isn't anger loud enough to drown out fear. It's fearlessness with no hatred in it. Guru Tegh Bahadur, the ninth Guru, puts it in one line near the end of the Granth, in plain English, not word for word: the wise one frightens no one, and fears no one. Both halves count. Fearing no one but frightening everyone isn't the picture. Neither is frightening no one only because you're too scared to stand up. And Maru's hymns keep pointing past the battlefield, to the fear inside a person, of loss, of being judged, of dying, and to the Name as the ground to stand on. So the raga of battle is also a raga of steadiness. That's today's line: courage.
screen: `A RAGA FOR THE EVE OF BATTLE.` · `NIRBHAU AND NIRVAIR, SIDE BY SIDE.` · `FRIGHTEN NO ONE, FEAR NO ONE.` · `THE FEAR INSIDE, THE GROUND TO STAND ON.` · then, large: `COURAGE.`

segments.voice: Plant your feet flat on the floor, feel their weight, and let your back be tall. Bring to mind one thing you've been putting off because it scares you a little, a phone call, an honest no, and look at it from where you sit without solving it: breathe in and feel the ground, breathe out and let go of any blame attached to it. If you pray, say Waheguru on the out-breath; if you don't, keep your feet planted and your breath steady.
Raga Maru. The raga tradition remembers being sung before battle, whose courage, in the Granth's terms, is without fear and without hate. Today's word.
Your line: courage. Without fear, and without making anyone else afraid. That makes a week.

chat.says: If Maru was sung before battle, does Sikh courage mean being angry enough not to fear?
options: No. The Granth pairs without fear and without hate: fear no one, frighten no one.
Yes. Anger is the fuel that lets a warrior forget fear on the field.
No. Courage means never facing anyone, so nobody gets frightened.
